name: Jaqaru
catalog_quote: Stress in Jaqaru is non-phonemic. It normally occurs on the penultimate vowel of the word and is frequently accompanied by a rise in pitch. In words of three vowels or more, a secondary stress occurs before the main stress. Hardman (1966:26).Vowel length is phonemic: c'aka 'bone' vs. c'a:ka 'chest'.

audit.reasoning: Quote check: both deciding texts are confirmed in held files — Hardman 1969's sentence verbatim on PDF p. 3 of the held ERIC scan, and the StressTyp2 passage verbatim in the held StressTyp2.sqlite (lect 152, passage 1118). But the classification ultimately rests on a database paraphrase of Hardman 1966:26 plus a one-sentence conference handout; none of Hardman's three grammars is held, so 'best available held' = no. Penultimate default is secure across every source seen (Hardman 1966 via StressTyp2, Hardman 1969, Cerrón-Palomino 1994, Walker 2010). The 'strict' flag is the exposed part: the record's own Walker quotation already reports antepenultimate stress in consonant-final loans, StressTyp2's Hardman paraphrase says 'normally', and Cerrón-Palomino 1994 (fetched sources now, pp. 76-77) states the accent is 'básicamente' penultimate but sensitive to underlying form and word-internal structure, with antepenultimate loans

Also read: Rachel Walker, "Vowel Fission in Jaqaru", LSA Annual Meeting Extended Abstr…
sources.quote: Hardman-de-Bautista 1969:3 (of Jaqaru, Kawki, and Aymara): "Stress, on the penultimate syllable of a word, is not phonemic in any of the languages". Corroborating, Walker (LSA extended abstract, p.1): "Stress in Jaqaru is usually penultimate, but it is antepenultimate in loans that were consonant-final and stressed on the penult in the donor language. ... When these loans are suffixed, stress shifts to the penult." (Walker's data credited to Cerrón-Palomino 2000, Lingüística Aimara.)

sources.quote: p.76: the accentual regime 'es básicamente llano o grave' (penultimate); many trisyllables carry a secondary accent with lengthening on the first syllable ([a:páka] 'anciana', [su:rúma] 'ladera') while others do not ([atpána], [mačáqa]). p.77: 'la acentuación jacaru parece ser sensible tanto a la forma subyacente de las palabras como a la estructura interna de las mismas'; consonant-final loans from Quechua and Spanish, after adding a paragogic vowel, 'mantienen la acentuación grave originaria. Así, por ejemplo, shúqushu ... háwasha' (i.e. surface antepenultimate); the two syllables of agentiv
sources.note: Independent phonologist's statement on Jaqaru accent (§6, pp. 76-77): basically penultimate but with antepenultimate consonant-final loans and morphology-sensitive cases — bears directly on the 'strict' flag.
